newsitem.title: USA: Perry advice to next Pentagon chief - hit the road.
newsitem.headline: Perry advice to next Pentagon chief - hit the road.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry, who is leaving his job after flying 650,000 miles in less than three years, has some advice for his successor: travel is the key to promoting world peace.

By far the most travelled Pentagon chief ever, Perry told reporters flying home with him from a global trip this week that visits to old allies and young democracies like Russia and other former Soviet and East Bloc states are a must.

"Any future secretary who has the same view that most secretaries have had, that they ought to maintain working relationships with their counterparts, will have to deal with 60 (countries) instead of 20," he said.

"And therefore they will have to do more travelling," he said over the whine of four jet engines aboard an Air Force C-17 that took him in seven days to Italy, Bosnia, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Japan and California.
Perry, 69, has resigned and administration sources said on Thursday that President Bill Clinton would nominate former Republican Sen. William Cohen of Maine to succeed him.

"I have continued to believe that this developing personal working relationships -- in particular (with defence ministers) but to a lesser extent prime ministers and foreign ministers -- is a very important part of my job," he said.

"My experience is that it has paid off in very important ways," Perry added, noting that he now has good ties with Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov just as he had with Rodionov's predecessor, Pavel Grachev.

"I don't find these trips tiring. I really get a great deal of satisfaction, draw a lot of energy and a lot of inspiration from being out in the field and meeting our troops," said Perry, a millionaire and a former mathematics professor at Stanford University in California.

He travels in three different types of aircraft -- two of which can refuel in the air -- and has spent more timne cultivating contacts in former Communist states such as Russia, Ukraine and Khazakstan than long-time NATO allies.
He suggested his successors might not have to travel quite as much now that "start-up" work is over.

Since February of 1994 when he was sworn in, Perry has paid four visits just to the former Soviet nuclear missile base at Pervomaisk in Khazakstan, the most recent to plant sunflowers over a now-empty intercontinental missile silo.
His trips are packed with work and leave him little time for sight-seeing. He sleeps in the air on long legs and favours the C-17 because there are bunks for his staff.
"On these trips, we don't sit around and read magazines," he said. "I take my office with me. It's a very good way for the staff to develop close working relationships."
The C-17 carries a specially inserted aluminum travel trailer dubbed "The Silver Bullet." The secretary uses it as office and bedroom.
Perry, who is very popular with the U.S. military, has brought major changes at the Pentagion including money-saving reforms in the way it develops and buys weapons systems.

He has come under criticism in the past year for two terrorist bombings in Saudi Arabia that killed 24 U.S. soldiers and for U.S. delays in announcing American troops would take part in a new peacekeeping force in Bosnia.
But Perry said every high office-holder must face "the critics who are out there, some of them well-meaning, some of them not well-meaning, who can and will criticise every decision you make."
He is expected to return to Stanford but said he would probably write a book first, adding: "What I would like to do is write, read, think, do some teaching and listen to Mozart."
